extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate/graduate students studying complex analysis (problem-solving)
extracted.subtask_description: A collection of exercise statements and hints from an appendix on elementary complex analysis covering definitions, theorems, and standard conventions used to produce correct solutions (holomorphicity, contour integrals, series, residues, conformal maps, harmonic functions, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition — complex differentiability in C^n
rubrics_metrics.description: We say that f is complex differentiable at z if there exists a complex linear mapping L : C^n → C such that lim_{ξ→0} (f(z+ξ) − f(z) − L(ξ))/|ξ| = 0. In this case we write f'(z) for it and call f' (z) the complex derivative of f at z. Its matrix is called the complex Jacobian matrix of f at z.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the primary definition to check when asserting complex differentiability in several variables; solutions should produce or use the linear map L (Jacobian) and verify the stated limit. (Problem 4 uses only Section B1 material.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Real-Jacobian block condition for complex differentiability (C^n ↔ R^{2n})
rubrics_metrics.description: f is complex differentiable at z iff f_R (the 2n-real-variable version of f) is differentiable at the corresponding real point and the real 2-by-2n Jacobian J satisfies, in block form, ( 0  -1 ; 1  0 ) J = J ( 0  -I ; I 0 ) (with appropriate block dimensions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem 4(a) asks to prove equivalence and to check the precise block-matrix relation; use the identification of complex multiplication with the 2×2 real matrix (0 -1; 1 0) and interpret blocks as n×n real matrices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Holomorphic equivalence in C^n (differentiable ⇔ holomorphic ⇔ C^∞ + Jacobian condition)
rubrics_metrics.description: f is complex differentiable at every point of an open set of C^n iff f is holomorphic on the open set, iff f_R is C^∞ on the open set and its real Jacobian satisfies the block condition from (a) at every point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem 4(b) requires using definitions and results from Section B15; when proving holomorphicity, one may show C^∞ regularity and the Jacobian condition or vice versa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stereographic projection — definition and inverse formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: Stereographic projection ϕ maps a point (x1,x2,x3) on the unit sphere S (excluding north pole (0,0,1)) to a complex number z = (x1 + i x2)/(1 − x3). The inverse ϕ^{-1}(z) gives explicit formulas for x1,x2,x3 in terms of z and ormulaul expressions are provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problems 5–8 ask to show ϕ is one-to-one and onto C (with inverse), that the inverse is given by rational formulas, that inverse images lie on straight lines in R^3 with the north pole, and that ϕ sends lines/circles in C to circles (intersections of S with planes in R^3). Use the explicit formulas and geometry for proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convention — orientation of circle integrals
rubrics_metrics.description: In complex line integrals taken over circles, it is understood that the circle is a standard one, traced out counterclockwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this orientation whenever evaluating integrals over 'standard' circles in problems (e.g., residues, Cauchy integrals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Cauchy Integral Theorem in a disk and its consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems 9–35 make use of the Cauchy Integral Theorem in a disk and its immediate consequences and its implications for Taylor series and the Argument Principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When solving related problems, employ Cauchy's integral formula, estimates for derivatives, Taylor expansions about centers in disks, and the Argument Principle to count zeros/poles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entire function properties and Liouville-type arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems involving entire functions often require proving constancy under growth or value constraints (e.g., functions with certain symmetries or boundedness properties, or with constraints on real/imaginary axis values).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical methods: apply Liouville's theorem, Schwarz reflection/symmetry arguments, consider F'(z)/F(z) to show an exponential representation, or use growth estimates to show polynomiality (Problem 22).

rubrics_metrics.name: Schwarz's Lemma statement and equality case
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is analytic on |z|<1 with f(0)=0 and |f(z)|≤1, then |f(z)|≤|z| and |f'(0)|≤1; equality in these inequalities holds only if f(z)=cz with c a constant of absolute value 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem 36 asks to prove the lemma by considering f(z)/z; verify both the inequality and the characterization of the equality case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Schwarz's Lemma for extremal-type problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply Schwarz's Lemma (and its variants) to bound values or derivatives of analytic maps on the unit disk, and to deduce sharpness/equality conditions for extremal problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problems 37–39 illustrate applications: e.g., bounding f(log 2) given constraints, or relating conformal maps to disk automorphisms and extremal quantities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rouché's Theorem — hypotheses and conclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Given analytic f and g on an open disk and a piecewise C^1 closed curve Γ in the disk such that f and g are nowhere zero on Γ and |g(z)/f(z)|<1 on Γ, then Γ encloses the same number of zeros of f as of f+g (counted with multiplicity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem 40 outlines a proof strategy via mapping g/f and the Argument Principle. Use Rouché's theorem to count zeros in regions (Problems 41–44, Fundamental Theorem of Algebra).

rubrics_metrics.name: Residue Theorem and method of residues
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the Residue Theorem to evaluate complex contour integrals and to compute real definite integrals via contour integration by identifying residues of enclosed singularities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problems 45–50 exercise evaluating complex integrals and real improper integrals by residues; ensure correct identification of poles, orders, and residues, and use the standard counterclockwise orientation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laurent series expansions and regions of validity
rubrics_metrics.description: A function analytic in an annulus has a Laurent expansion ∑_{n=-∞}^∞ c_n z^n valid in that annulus; different annular regions yield different Laurent series. Determine coefficients and maximal regions of validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problems 51–54 ask for explicit expansions, determination of number of expansions, annuli of convergence, and linking to Bernoulli numbers for specific expansions (e.g., cot z).

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform convergence on compact sets and normal families
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequence of functions converges uniformly on compact sets in U if for each compact K⊂U and each ε>0 there is N with |f_n−f|<ε on K for n≥N. A set E of analytic functions on U is a normal family if it is uniformly bounded on each compact subset of U.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problems 55–60 develop consequences: uniform limit of analytic functions is analytic (55); derivatives converge under uniform convergence of derivatives (56); Hurwitz's Theorem (57) about limits of nowhere-zero functions; equicontinuity and Arzelà–Ascoli arguments (59–60).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hurwitz's Theorem (limit of nowhere-zero analytic functions)
rubrics_metrics.description: If {f_n} is a sequence of nowhere-zero analytic functions on U converging uniformly on compact sets to f, then either f is nowhere zero or f is identically zero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem 57: apply zeros-counting/argument principles and normal-family arguments; useful when passing to limits in families of analytic maps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linear fractional transformations (Mobius maps) — matrix representation and sphere extension
rubrics_metrics.description: A linear fractional transformation L(z) = (a z + b)/(c z + d) corresponds to the 2×2 matrix [a b; c d] (ad−bc≠0). Extend L to the Riemann sphere S = C ∪ {∞} by setting L(−d/c)=∞ and L(∞)=a/c when c≠0. Composition corresponds to matrix multiplication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problems 61–66: check one-one, onto properties, inverse formula, extension to S, and uniqueness by fixing three points. Use matrix algebra for composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of Mobius maps preserving half-plane or unit disk
rubrics_metrics.description: Mobius maps carrying the upper half-plane to itself correspond to real-coefficient matrices with ad−bc>0; those carrying the unit disk to itself correspond to matrices of the form [α β; rac{β̄}{?} rac{ᾱ}{?}] with the stated norm condition (see Problem 68).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problems 67–68: to show a map preserves these domains, check matrix conditions and/or compose with stereographic projection; conversely, every such self-map arises from such matrices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-ratio invariance under linear fractional transformations
rubrics_metrics.description: The cross ratio (z1,z2,z3,z4) is invariant under any linear fractional transformation T: (T z1, T z2, T z3, T z4) = (z1,z2,z3,z4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem 66: use the unique LFT sending z2,z3,z4 to 1,0,∞ and check image of z1; invariance is used to characterize quadruples and map configurations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmonic functions — relation to analytic functions and conjugates
rubrics_metrics.description: If f=u+iv is analytic then u and v are harmonic. A conjugate harmonic function v for u (making u+iv analytic) is unique up to an additive constant; on simply connected regions every harmonic function has a conjugate (hence is locally the real part of an analytic function).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problems 69–72: prove harmonicity from Cauchy–Riemann, uniqueness and existence (bounded/simple regions), and consequences like C^∞ regularity of harmonic functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maximum principle and mean-value property for harmonic functions
rubrics_metrics.description: A harmonic function on a region cannot attain a local maximum unless it is constant; harmonic functions satisfy mean value properties (value at center is average on circle). Positive harmonic functions on R^2 are constant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problems 74–76: use mean-value formula and maximum principle to deduce constancy results and image properties of harmonic maps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vector-valued holomorphic functions and Jacobian block structure
rubrics_metrics.description: For f: U ⊂ C^n → C^m complex differentiable at z, the real Jacobian J of f_R satisfies block relations analogous to the scalar case: ( 0 -I ; I 0 ) J = J ( 0 -I ; I 0 ), and JC (complex Jacobian) decomposes as Re JC + i Im JC with J = [Re JC  -Im JC; Im JC  Re JC].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problems 78–79: use componentwise differentiability, decompose JC into real/imaginary parts, and verify composition rule: complex Jacobian of g∘f equals product of Jacobians at respective points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex inverse and implicit function theorems (versions for holomorphic maps)
rubrics_metrics.description: State and prove complex-variable versions of the real-variable Inverse Function Theorem and Implicit Function Theorem for holomorphic maps (Problems 80–81).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate the real theorems into complex form using complex Jacobian (nonvanishing determinant) and holomorphicity hypotheses; prove local invertibility and solvability with holomorphic dependence.
